name: Chin implant / genioplasty

card.summary: Two ways to build out the chin, a placed implant or a cut-and-slid piece of the jawbone; routine cosmetic and orthognathic surgery with the larger changes coming from bone.
card.aka: sliding genioplasty, chin extension, mentoplasty, chin augmentation
card.note: Fixes chin position, not the bite; numbness, implant shifting or bone changes and asymmetry are documented risks.

quick.overview:
Chin augmentation changes the underlying structure of the chin to balance the rest of the face. The two main surgical approaches are an implant placed over the bone and a sliding genioplasty, in which a section of the lower jawbone is cut and moved forward, back, up or down. It is often done alongside a nose operation or jaw surgery.

On looksmaxxing forums the chin is a frequent target, with threads comparing genioplasty with bimax, asking how many millimetres are needed and discussing recovery and removal. Published reviews cover techniques, materials, stability and complications; there is little head-to-head research on which approach produces the best appearance.
quick.mechanism: An implant adds volume to the front of the chin through an incision inside the lip or under the chin. A sliding genioplasty cuts a horseshoe-shaped piece of bone from the lower edge of the jaw, repositions it and fixes it with plates and screws, so the tissue attached to it moves too.
quick.risks: Reported problems include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip or chin numbness, infection, implant displacement or bone changes under implants, nerve injury and asymmetry. Surgery is performed by plastic, facial plastic or oral and maxillofacial surgeons as regulated cosmetic or orthognathic surgery.

lead: Chin augmentation, also called mentoplasty or genioplasty, changes the underlying structure of the chin so that it balances the nose, lips and jawline in profile and front view. It can add projection with an implant, move the chin forward, back, up or down by cutting and repositioning the bone, or narrow and reshape it.[1][18] People choose it to make a recessed chin project further, to lengthen a short lower third of the face, to strengthen the jawline and neck-chin contour, or to reduce a prominent chin.[1][18]

There are two surgical families. In a sliding genioplasty, a horseshoe-shaped piece of the lower edge of the jaw is cut free, moved and fixed in its new position with plates and screws or wires, carrying the attached soft tissue with it.[1] In implant (alloplastic) augmentation, a shaped implant is placed in a pocket over the bone through an incision inside the mouth or under the chin.[1] Non-surgical options include injectable fillers.[1] Reviews describe the bone-based operation as more flexible and generally capable of larger or three-dimensional changes, and the implant as the simpler procedure; neither corrects the bite.[1][5]

Genioplasty is widely performed on its own and alongside rhinoplasty, facelifts and orthognathic (jaw) surgery, and a 2025 review notes it is also used for facial asymmetry and, combined with jaw advancement, for obstructive sleep apnea.[2][3][18] On looksmax.org the chin is one of the most discussed surgical targets, with threads on how many millimetres of advancement to seek, genioplasty versus double-jaw surgery, and recovery and removal experiences.[14][17]

chain: Implant adds volume, or osteotomy moves the chin bone
Chin sits further forward, lower or higher relative to nose, lips and jaw
angle.text: The operation physically changes where the front of the jaw sits, so the change in profile is structural and permanent in the sense that it does not depend on daily upkeep. Bone-based movement can alter projection, height and width; implants add projection and fullness. Surgeons often plan it together with nose or jaw work so the whole profile fits together.

paras: The chin is a main anchor of the facial profile. Surgeons assess it in relation to the nose, lips, lower facial height and the position of the jaws, and the review literature stresses evaluating the chin on its own merit as well as in the context of the whole face.[3] Wikipedia describes chin augmentation as improving projection and height and as commonly paired with rhinoplasty; it also notes that a small chin together with a significant overbite may call for orthognathic surgery instead of, or in addition to, a chin procedure.[1]

A 2025 review lists the aims of genioplasty as correcting microgenia (a small or recessed chin), macrogenia (an excessive chin), asymmetry, and, in selected cases, airway-related problems.[18] Because the operation changes bone or implant position rather than soft tissue alone, proponents describe the results as stable and not requiring maintenance, whereas fillers are temporary.[1][18]

Sliding genioplasty: a horseshoe-shaped piece of bone is cut from the lower edge of the mandible below the nerve openings and moved forward to add projection or backward to reduce it, then fixed with a titanium plate and screws or with fine wires.[1] The 2025 review lists advancement for microgenia, setback for a prominent chin, vertical lengthening using bone grafting or distraction, vertical reduction by removing bone, and narrowing, which is common in Asian aesthetic surgery.[18] The T-osteotomy or mini V-line, developed by Korean surgeons, narrows and lengthens the chin by a few millimetres, with the mentalis muscle carefully reattached because it controls lower-lip and chin movement.[1][18]

Implants: silicone is soft and smooth, does not bond to tissue, can shift and may be associated with bone resorption but is easy to remove; porous polyethylene (Medpor) allows tissue ingrowth and is harder to remove; ePTFE (Gore-Tex) is flexible and often screwed to the bone.[1] A review of facial implants in men notes that alloplastic implants provide the most predictable hard-tissue augmentation and discusses their most common and severe complications.[7] Patient-specific implants made from computer planning, including PEEK, are the subject of registered studies.[15][16]

Non-surgical and adjunct options: injectable fillers such as hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxyapatite last months to years, while permanent fillers such as free silicone have fallen out of favour because of migration, inflammation and infection concerns.[1] The 2024 randomized trial cited below also tested autogenous fat as an augmentation material.[12]

Genioplasty is usually performed through an incision inside the lower lip, so no external scar results, although a skin incision under the chin is used for some implant placements.[1] Wikipedia notes that recovery involves minimising chewing, soft foods and liquids for a period, and that sliding genioplasty may be accompanied by intermaxillary fixation for three to four weeks in some practices.[1] Technical points emphasised in the 2025 review include preserving the mental nerve, using rigid fixation with pre-bent absorbable plates or titanium screws, and tensioning the mentalis muscle to avoid chin ptosis and lower-lip incompetence.[18]

Operating methods for correcting a small chin and for mandibular surgery were described in two 1957 papers by Trauner and Obwegeser on the correction of prognathism and retrognathism with consideration of genioplasty.[8][9] Hugo Obwegeser is widely credited in the surgical literature with introducing intraoral osseous genioplasty in this period. A 1958 report by Aufricht on combined nose and chin surgery based on decades of experience is cited by Wikipedia as an early plastic-surgery account.[1]

A 1988 review described implants as the most commonly used chin procedure and osteotomy as the technique offering the greatest flexibility, and a 1989 review by a plastic surgeon described performing both operations and called for greater use of genioplasty among aesthetic surgeons.[4][5] In 1990 Guyuron and Raszewski compared bone-based and implant-based approaches, and in 2014 Lee and colleagues described the T-osteotomy method, standardised further in 2015.[1] Contemporary work includes resorbable fixation, piezoelectric bone cutting and computer-guided or patient-specific approaches.[10][11][12][15][16]

A 2025 review reports that long-term results are stable with minimal relapse when appropriate rigid fixation is used, citing a study of 62 patients who had advancement, setback or no sagittal change that found no significant relapse and a strong correlation between hard- and soft-tissue movement, particularly for setbacks.[18] The same review cites a series of 208 patients with a 5.8 percent complication rate, all temporary sensory loss, and 92.8 percent patient satisfaction, and states that studies generally report satisfaction above 90 percent.[18]

A 2024 review states that the soft tissues around the mandible tend to return toward their original position even when osteotomy segments are secure, which is a reason surgeons give for careful planning of movements.[2] A 2023 review of contemporary genioplasty covers techniques, applications, stability, osteosynthesis and complications.[3] Head-to-head comparison of implants and osteotomy for appearance is limited to a small number of trials and registered studies.[12][15]

Controlled studies on genioplasty are mostly technical. A randomised trial compared two types of high labial incision, a randomised study examined piezosurgery, and a clinical study of 20 patients tested resorbable fixation, with most genial movements being advancements.[6][10][11] A 2024 randomised controlled trial evaluated soft-tissue profile changes after autogenous fat or onlay PEEK augmentation versus sliding genioplasty for a deficient chin.[12]

A study of 1,034 patients who underwent orthognathic surgery examined neurosensory function in the mental nerve region at two years after mandibular osteotomies including genioplasty.[13] Registered studies compare patient-specific alloplastic chin implants with computer-guided genioplasty and test the accuracy of patient-specific PEEK implants for chin deficiency.[15][16]

Common and usually minor effects include swelling, hematoma and temporary lip weakness or numbness; less common are infection, bony changes under the implant, implant displacement, asymmetry and nerve damage.[1] Silicone implants may shift or erode bone, and donor bone grafts have been linked to a higher infection rate.[1] Wikipedia cites White and Dufresne (2011) as emphasising that surgeon experience helps reduce complications.[1]

Inferior alveolar and mental nerve function after mandibular osteotomies has been studied directly: a 1998 study reported measurable neurosensory deficits at two years after the sagittal split operation and also examined genioplasty.[13] The 2025 review names preservation of the mental nerve and correct muscle reattachment as central to avoiding sensory loss and lip or chin soft-tissue problems.[18]

Chin surgery is a staple of surgical discussion on looksmax.org. Threads ask whether a chin problem is better handled by genioplasty or by double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery, and members share planning measurements, recovery experiences and implant-removal stories.[14][17] One member reports that a surgeon proposed about 4 to 5 mm of advancement for an average chin and offered to extend the chin vertically to improve facial thirds.[17]

The Wikipedia article attributes the procedure's popularity to its relatively easy recovery and visible effect on the profile.[1] In the forums the chin is often framed as part of the lower third and the jaw-to-neck line, which is why genioplasty is frequently discussed alongside jaw implants, fillers and bimaxillary surgery.[14]

Aufricht reports combined nose and chin surgery from long experience (as cited by Wikipedia).[1]
A review describes implants as the most commonly used chin procedure and osteotomy as the most flexible.[5]
A plastic surgeon's review argues for greater use of genioplasty in aesthetic practice.[4]
Guyuron and Raszewski compare osteoplastic and alloplastic genioplasty (as cited by Wikipedia).[1]
A study of nerve function after mandibular osteotomies including genioplasty reports outcomes at two years.[13]
A study evaluates resorbable fixation in genioplasty.[10]
Lee and colleagues describe the T-osteotomy (mini V-line) for narrowing and lengthening the chin.[1]
A randomised trial compares fat or PEEK onlay with sliding genioplasty.[12]
A review of current concepts summarises techniques, indications and stability data.[18]

lore.intro: Chin surgery is one of the most frequently discussed procedures on looksmaxxing forums, with threads on genioplasty versus bimax, millimetre targets, recovery diets and complications.[14][17]

claims.claim: Sliding genioplasty gives a bigger, more reliable change than a chin implant.
claims.believers: Forum members weigh genioplasty against implants and double-jaw surgery when asking how to fix a recessed chin.[14]
claims.experts: Reviews describe osteotomy as offering the greatest flexibility and potential for significant modification of chin form, while implants are the more commonly used and simpler option.[1][5]

claims.claim: A few millimetres of advancement is enough for an average chin.
claims.believers: One member reports his surgeon suggesting 4 to 5 mm for an average chin and offering more on request.[17]
claims.experts: Reviews emphasise objective evaluation of the chin on its own merit and note the tendency of soft tissue to return toward its original position, but no source sets a standard distance.[2][3]

claims.claim: A chin procedure alone may not solve a profile problem caused by the jaws.
claims.believers: A poster asks whether their issue is lower third only or maxilla and mandible position and whether genioplasty alone would fix it.[14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says genioplasty does not correct the bite and that cases with a small chin and large overbite may need orthognathic surgery.[1]

claims.claim: Genioplasty results are permanent and stable.
claims.believers: Members considering surgery commonly treat bone movement as a one-time, lasting change, in contrast with fillers.[14]
claims.experts: A 2025 review reports stable long-term results with minimal relapse when rigid fixation is used, while a 2024 review notes soft tissue tends to drift back toward its original position.[18][2]

claims.claim: Implants are the lower-risk option because no bone is cut.
claims.believers: Forum discussion often presents implants as the lighter operation and genioplasty as the bigger commitment.[14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists implant shifting, bone resorption under silicone and infection among implant risks, and a review of male facial implants discusses their most common and severe complications; osteotomy carries nerve-related numbness risks.[1][7][13]

claims.claim: Genioplasty can also extend or narrow the chin, not only push it forward.
claims.believers: Members report surgeons offering vertical lengthening to improve facial thirds.[17]
claims.experts: A 2025 review lists vertical lengthening, reduction and narrowing alongside advancement and setback.[18]
